Hungary's Oil & Gas Output Hit by Measles Outbreak Among Workers

Budapest, June 13—A measles outbreak among oil and gas industry workers in Hungary has disrupted operations at several extraction and processing sites, according to industry officials and union representatives.

At least 120 employees have tested positive for measles since late May at facilities operated by Danube Energy Resources and Magyar Fuel Partners in central and southern Hungary, forcing temporary shutdowns and reduced staffing. The Hungarian Petroleum Workers’ Union said Thursday that more than 400 workers are currently in quarantine, citing figures provided by local health authorities.

“Production at our Paks refinery is currently running at approximately 60% capacity due to staff shortages,” said Béla Kovács, spokesperson for Danube Energy Resources. “We are prioritizing workforce safety and closely monitoring the situation with public health officials.”

The outbreak has raised concerns about possible delays to scheduled fuel shipments and maintenance projects. According to the Hungarian Oil & Gas Association, daily crude output from the affected regions has fallen by roughly 18% compared to May averages.

“We are working with member companies to implement enhanced hygiene protocols and vaccination drives,” said association president Ilona Szabó. “The health of our workers is paramount, but we recognize the impact this is having on overall sector performance.”

Union officials say many workers had not received measles booster vaccinations, which contributed to the rapid spread of the disease at communal living quarters and worksites. “This outbreak highlights the urgent need for better preventive healthcare measures in our industry,” said union leader Gábor Farkas.

Health authorities have not set a date for lifting quarantine measures, and officials warn that further disruptions are possible if new cases continue to emerge. The Oil & Gas Association has urged companies to review contingency plans as the situation develops.
